```{r load}
library(starling)
library(mudnester)   # clean_the_nest() and the clutch_* datasets
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

aviary_cols <- c(satin = "#325D88", chestnut = "#86251C", wattle = "#D8A31A",
                 evergreen = "#08403B", mud = "#A67D4C", slate = "#3E3F3A")
```

## (*)> Overview

This vignette demonstrates the complete `starling` probabilistic record linkage
workflow (Fellegi-Sunter scoring [3], run through `reclin2` [4]): pre-linkage audit, blocking, threshold sensitivity analysis, linkage,
post-linkage validation, and the analysis the linkage exists to serve. The
scenario mirrors a routine SCPHU task and the design of a regional Queensland
linkage study of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness [1]: link a notifiable-disease
linelist to the Australian Immunisation Register
(AIR) to establish COVID-19 vaccination status at onset, link the same
linelist to hospital admissions to establish severity, and estimate vaccine
effectiveness (VE) against hospitalisation.

The data are three of the `clutch` teaching datasets shipped in `mudnester`:

| Dataset | Rows | Role here |
|---|---|---|
| `clutch_cases` | `r format(nrow(clutch_cases), big.mark = ",")` | `data_x`: notified COVID-19, influenza, RSV and measles cases |
| `clutch_air` | `r format(nrow(clutch_air), big.mark = ",")` | `data_y` (vaccination): one row per vaccine encounter |
| `clutch_hospital` | `r format(nrow(clutch_hospital), big.mark = ",")` | `data_y` (hospitalisation): one row per episode of care |

All three are synthetic -- no real person data -- with the identifier errors
real extracts carry (typos, nicknames, swapped day/month, missing and
household-shared Medicare numbers). Every record also carries a `truth_id`,
which real data never has. It is used here only to *grade* the linkage.

***

## (*)> Step 0: Clean both sides the same way

`mudnester::clean_the_nest()` standardises every source into the same schema.
Roughly one notification in ten has no onset date, so the specimen date stands
in for it first -- `murmuration()` anchors every event window on `event_date`.

```{r clean}
cases_raw <- clutch_cases |>
  mutate(
    onset_imputed = is.na(onset_date),                  # keep a flag
    onset_date    = coalesce(onset_date, specimen_date) # fall back to the specimen date
  )

cases_clean <- clean_the_nest(
  cases_raw,
  data_type   = "cases",
  drop_eggs   = TRUE,
  id_var      = "notification_id",
  diagnosis   = "condition",
  lettername1 = "first_name",
  lettername2 = "surname",
  dob         = "date_of_birth",
  gender      = "sex",
  postcode    = "postcode",
  medicare    = "medicare_number",
  onset_date  = "onset_date",
  keep_vars   = c("truth_id", "onset_imputed")
)
```

> **(*)> One vaccine type at a time.** Filter the AIR extract to the vaccine
> you are studying before `clean_the_nest(lie_nest_flat = TRUE)` and
> `murmuration()`. Otherwise `vax_date_1`, `vax_date_2`, ... interleave every
> vaccine the person has had -- influenza, zoster, MMR -- and the dose counts
> and `vaccination_status` mean "any vaccine", not "a COVID-19 dose". One
> vaccine per call is also how `murmuration()` is designed (`?murmuration`,
> "Linking one cohort to several event streams").

```{r clean-air}
air_covid_raw <- clutch_air |>
  filter(antigen == "COVID-19")   # the one vaccine this analysis is about

air_covid <- clean_the_nest(
  air_covid_raw,
  data_type     = "vaccination",
  lie_nest_flat = TRUE,          # one row per person: vax_date_1, vax_type_1, ...
  drop_eggs     = TRUE,
  id_var        = "air_id",
  lettername1   = "given_name",
  lettername2   = "family_name",
  dob           = "date_of_birth",
  gender        = "sex",
  postcode      = "postcode",
  medicare      = "medicare_card",
  medicare_irn  = "medicare_irn",  # the AIR stores the IRN in its own column
  vax_type      = "antigen",
  vax_date      = "date_of_service",
  keep_vars     = "truth_id"
)

cases_clean |>
  count(diagnosis)
c(covid_doses = nrow(air_covid_raw), people_with_a_covid_dose = nrow(air_covid))
```

***

## (*)> Step 1: Pre-linkage audit with `preflight()`

Before generating a single candidate pair, `preflight()` checks completeness
of the linkage variables, duplicate identifiers, date plausibility, Medicare
validity, name quality and factor-level consistency across both datasets.

```{r preflight}
cases_covid_clean <- cases_clean |>
  filter(diagnosis == "COVID-19")

audit <- preflight(
  data1        = cases_covid_clean,
  data2        = air_covid,
  linkage_vars = c("lettername1", "lettername2", "dob", "medicare10"),
  id_col1      = "id_var",
  id_col2      = "id_var",
  date_cols    = c("dob", "onset_date"),
  medicare_col = "medicare10",
  verbose      = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(audit$completeness, caption = "Completeness of the linkage variables")
audit$flags
```

The row to notice is Medicare: it is missing on
`r round(100 * mean(is.na(cases_covid_clean$medicare10)))`% of COVID-19
notifications but almost never on the AIR. That single fact shapes the score
distribution in Step 4.

***

## (*)> Step 2: Medicare checksum validation with `check_medicare()`

An invalid Medicare number that happens to resemble someone else's adds
spurious weight to a false pair. Setting it to `NA` is better: the EM
algorithm treats `NA` as "not observed" and it contributes nothing, positive
or negative.

```{r medicare}
cases_checked <- cases_clean |>
  check_medicare(medicare_col = "medicare10", output_col = "medicare_valid",
                 verbose = FALSE) |>
  mutate(medicare10 = if_else(medicare_valid %in% 0L, NA_character_, medicare10))

air_checked <- air_covid |>
  check_medicare(medicare_col = "medicare10", output_col = "medicare_valid",
                 verbose = FALSE) |>
  mutate(medicare10 = if_else(medicare_valid %in% 0L, NA_character_, medicare10))

bind_rows(
  cases_checked |> mutate(dataset = "clutch_cases"),
  air_checked   |> mutate(dataset = "clutch_air (COVID-19)")
) |>
  group_by(dataset) |>
  summarise(
    valid          = sum(medicare_valid %in% 1L),
    fails_checksum = sum(medicare_valid %in% 0L),
    missing        = sum(is.na(medicare_valid))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Medicare numbers after check_medicare(): invalid ones are set to NA")
```

***

## (*)> Step 3: Blocking variables with `flock()`

`murmuration()` only compares pairs that share a blocking key. Gender plus
birth year keeps nearly every true pair together at a fraction of the cost of
gender alone (see `vignette("pre-linkage-quality")` for the measured
trade-off).

```{r flock}
cases_blocked <- flock(cases_checked,
                       block1_vars    = c("gender", "birth_year"),
                       birth_year_col = "dob")
air_blocked   <- flock(air_checked,
                       block1_vars    = c("gender", "birth_year"),
                       birth_year_col = "dob")

cases_covid <- cases_blocked |>
  filter(diagnosis == "COVID-19")

c(covid_cases = nrow(cases_covid),
  air_people  = nrow(air_blocked),
  strata      = length(intersect(cases_covid$block1, air_blocked$block1)))
```

***

## (*)> Step 4: Look at the scores before trusting a threshold

The first run leaves `threshold_value` at the starling default of 16 and
keeps the full candidate-pairs table (`keep_pairs_pred = TRUE`) so it can be
inspected. The vaccination window counts a COVID-19 dose as current if it was
given 14--182 days before onset.

```{r link-16}
linked_16 <- murmuration(
  data_x          = cases_covid,     # one row per COVID-19 case
  data_y          = air_blocked,     # one row per AIR person, COVID-19 doses only
  linkage_type    = "cohort2event",  # a cohort linked to an event stream...
  event_type      = "vaccination",   # ...of vaccinations
  event_date      = "onset_date",    # each case's own anchor date
  id_var          = "id_var",        # the case identifier, kept on every row
  blocking_var    = "block1",        # only pairs of the same gender and birth year
  compare_vars    = c("lettername1", "lettername2", "dob", "medicare10"),
  # threshold_value not set: the default, 16
  vax_window      = list(days_before = 14, days_after = 0, lookback_days = 182),
  keep_pairs_pred = TRUE             # keep every scored pair for the plots
)
```

`perch()` sweeps candidate thresholds over the scored pairs without re-fitting
anything. With `plot = FALSE` it returns its table invisibly:

```{r perch}
pp_16 <- attr(linked_16, "pairs_pred") |>
  as.data.frame()

# the most a pair can score when Medicare is missing on one side
max_weight_no_medicare <- pp_16 |>
  filter(is.na(medicare10)) |>
  pull(weights) |>
  max()

sweep <- perch(pp_16,
               n_records_primary = nrow(cases_covid),
               thresholds        = seq(4, 20, by = 1),
               report            = FALSE,
               plot              = FALSE)

knitr::kable(sweep[, c("threshold", "n_above", "n_clerical", "link_rate", "reference")],
             caption = "Accepted pairs and clerical burden at each candidate threshold")
```

The count of accepted pairs barely moves between about 7 and 10, then falls
away in steps above 10. The first step is the Medicare effect: a true pair whose
Medicare number is missing on one side can score at most the name and
date-of-birth weights, which here sum to about
`r round(max_weight_no_medicare, 1)`. At 16
every one of those true pairs is thrown away, and so is every true pair whose
card was reissued between the two records (a different tenth digit; see
`vignette("threshold-selection")`, which measures both).

```{r plot-16, fig.cap = "Candidate-pair weights at the default threshold of 16. The upper cluster (all four fields agree) sits above 16; the true matches with a reissued card or no Medicare number on one side sit between about 10 and 13, entirely below the line."}
murmuration_plot(linked_16, max_levels = 10)
```

The valley between the non-match cloud and the lower match cluster sits near
8, so the linkage is re-run there -- the same look-before-fixing discipline an
infant immunisation coverage study applied to its birth-register matching [2]. The starling default and the AIHW/WADLU
and PHRN benchmarks in the `perch()` table all assume a five-variable key with
a Medicare number present and current on both sides; with four variables and
frequent Medicare gaps the scale is simply lower.

| Range | Source | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 10--20 | AIHW / WA Data Linkage Unit | Clerical review zone |
| 15--20 | PHRN | Operational target for <0.5% false-match rate (full variable set) |
| 16 | starling default | Calibrated for 5 comparison variables with an agreeing Medicare number |

***

## (*)> Step 5: Probabilistic linkage with `murmuration()`

```{r link-8}
linked_cov <- murmuration(
  data_x          = cases_covid,     # one row per COVID-19 case
  data_y          = air_blocked,     # one row per AIR person, COVID-19 doses only
  linkage_type    = "cohort2event",
  event_type      = "vaccination",
  event_date      = "onset_date",    # the window is measured back from onset
  id_var          = "id_var",
  blocking_var    = "block1",        # gender + birth year
  compare_vars    = c("lettername1", "lettername2", "dob", "medicare10"),
  threshold_value = 8,               # the valley seen in Step 4
  vax_window      = list(days_before = 14,     # a dose counts from 14 days old...
                         days_after = 0,
                         lookback_days = 182), # ...until 182 days old
  suffix          = "_cov",          # tag every column this call adds
  keep_pairs_pred = TRUE
)

bind_rows(
  linked_16  |> summarise(threshold     = 16,
                          linked_to_air = sum(!is.na(id_var_y)),
                          current_dose  = sum(vaccination_status == "Vaccinated")),
  linked_cov |> summarise(threshold     = 8,
                          linked_to_air = sum(!is.na(id_var_y_cov)),
                          current_dose  = sum(vaccination_status_cov == "Vaccinated"))
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "COVID-19 cases linked to an AIR record, and with a dose 14-182 days before onset")
```

`suffix = "_cov"` tags every column this call contributed (`weights_cov`,
`id_var_y_cov`, `vaccination_status_cov`, `vax_date_1_cov`, ...) while the
case columns, including `id_var`, stay plain -- so the result can be joined to
the hospital linkage in Step 8 without collisions. The vaccination route
returns an ordinary, ungrouped data frame with one row per case. Alongside the
in-window `vax_date_*`/`vax_type_*` columns it adds:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `vaccination_status` | `"Vaccinated"` if any dose falls inside `vax_window`, otherwise `"Unvaccinated"` (including cases with no AIR record) |
| `vaccination_status_num` | The same as 1/0, ready for a model |
| `total_valid_vax` | Number of in-window doses |
| `first_vax_date`, `last_vax_date` (and `_type`) | Earliest and latest in-window dose |
| `tsv` | Days from the last in-window dose to `event_date`; 0 when unvaccinated |

"Vaccinated" below means `vaccination_status_cov == "Vaccinated"`.

```{r vax-status}
linked_cov |>
  count(vaccination_status_cov, total_valid_vax_cov, name = "cases") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "vaccination_status against the number of in-window doses (threshold 8)")
```

***

## (*)> Step 6: Visualise the final score distribution

```{r plot-8, fig.cap = "Linkage weight distribution at threshold 8, jittered by blocking stratum (gender + birth year). Above-threshold pairs are drawn as triangles."}
murmuration_plot(linked_cov, max_levels = 10, palette = "sch")
```

If the distribution is cleanly bimodal and the above-threshold count matches
expectations, this is normally as far as you need to go. If specific
borderline pairs deserve a human judgement, see
`vignette("clinical-linkage-review")` for `inspect_matches` and
`resume_from_pairs`.

***

## (*)> Step 7: Post-linkage validation against the truth

In production this step needs a clerical review sample. Here the matched AIR
record's `truth_id` can be compared with the case's directly.

```{r validate}
# the truth_id behind each matched AIR record -- used only to grade the links
air_truth <- air_blocked |>
  select(id_var_y_cov = id_var, truth_id_air = truth_id)

grading <- linked_cov |>
  left_join(air_truth, by = "id_var_y_cov") |>
  summarise(
    n_links   = sum(!is.na(id_var_y_cov)),
    n_correct = sum(truth_id == truth_id_air, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
n_links   <- grading$n_links
n_correct <- grading$n_correct
n_true    <- cases_covid |>
  filter(truth_id %in% air_blocked$truth_id) |>
  nrow()

tibble(
  measure = c("Accepted links", "Correct links", "Cases with a true AIR record",
              "Precision (%)", "Recall (%)"),
  value   = c(n_links, n_correct, n_true,
              round(100 * n_correct / n_links, 1),
              round(100 * n_correct / n_true, 1))
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### A note on cases with more than one candidate

Common names and family members who share a Medicare card and a birth year
can put a second AIR record above the threshold. `murmuration()` keeps the
highest-weighted candidate for each case (earlier releases kept the first in
`data_y` row order), so the precision recomputed from the candidate-pairs
table matches the linkage's own. The highest weight is usually, but not
always, the right person:

```{r multi-candidate}
# every candidate pair above the threshold, with both sides' truth_id
above <- attr(linked_cov, "pairs_pred") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(weights >= 8) |>
  select(row_x = .x, row_y = .y, weights) |>
  mutate(truth_x = cases_covid$truth_id[row_x],
         truth_y = air_blocked$truth_id[row_y])

# cases with two or more candidates
multi_x <- above |>
  count(row_x) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  pull(row_x)

# what murmuration() keeps: the highest-weighted candidate per case
best <- above |>
  arrange(desc(weights)) |>
  distinct(row_x, .keep_all = TRUE)

best_multi <- best |>
  filter(row_x %in% multi_x)

tibble(
  measure = c("Cases with 2+ candidates above 8",
              "  of which the highest-weighted candidate is the right person",
              "Precision of murmuration()'s links (%)",
              "Precision recomputed from the pairs, highest weight per case (%)"),
  value   = c(length(multi_x),
              sum(best_multi$truth_x == best_multi$truth_y),
              round(100 * n_correct / n_links, 1),
              round(100 * mean(best$truth_x == best$truth_y), 1))
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Where the highest weight is the wrong person, the cause is a near-tie between
two plausible people, not the threshold: a higher `threshold_value` drops most
of the second candidates only by also discarding true pairs that score in the
same range. Reviewing those cases (see `vignette("clinical-linkage-review")`)
resolves them without that cost, and where both records carry the IRN it
settles a family-member pair outright (see `vignette("pre-linkage-quality")`).

***

## (*)> Step 8: Linking the same cases to hospital admissions

The hospital extract codes sex as `"Male"`/`"Female"`, so it is recoded before
cleaning (otherwise no pair would ever share a block). Only acute episodes are
relevant; maternity and newborn episodes are left out. An admission counts as
disease-related if it starts between 7 days before and 14 days after onset,
and a death within 30 days of onset counts as a COVID-19 death.

```{r hospital-clean}
hosp_raw <- clutch_hospital |>
  filter(care_type == "Acute") |>                      # no maternity or newborn episodes
  mutate(sex = case_when(sex == "Male"   ~ "M",        # the hospital codes sex in full;
                         sex == "Female" ~ "F"))       # every other source uses M/F

hosp_clean <- clean_the_nest(
  hosp_raw,
  data_type      = "hospital",
  drop_eggs      = TRUE,
  id_var         = "ur_number",
  event_id_var   = "episode_id",
  lettername1    = "given_name",
  lettername2    = "family_name",
  dob            = "birth_date",
  gender         = "sex",
  postcode       = "postcode",
  medicare       = "medicare_no",
  admission_date = "admit_date",
  discharge_date = "separation_date",
  hospital       = "facility",
  icd_code       = "principal_diagnosis",
  drg            = "drg",
  icu_date       = "icu_date",
  icu_hours      = "icu_hours",
  dod            = "death_date",   # age at admission is derived from dob and admit_date
  keep_vars      = c("truth_id", "diagnosis_codes")
)

hosp_blocked <- hosp_clean |>
  check_medicare(medicare_col = "medicare10", output_col = "medicare_valid",
                 verbose = FALSE) |>
  mutate(medicare10 = if_else(medicare_valid %in% 0L, NA_character_, medicare10)) |>
  flock(block1_vars    = c("gender", "birth_year"),
        birth_year_col = "dob")
```

```{r hospital-link}
linked_hosp <- murmuration(
  data_x                    = cases_blocked,      # every case, all four conditions
  data_y                    = hosp_blocked,       # acute episodes
  linkage_type              = "cohort2event",
  event_type                = "hospitalisation",
  event_date                = "onset_date",
  id_var                    = "id_var",
  blocking_var              = "block1",           # gender + birth year
  compare_vars              = c("lettername1", "lettername2", "dob", "medicare10"),
  threshold_value           = 8,
  days_allowed_before_event = 7,                  # admitted up to 7 days before onset...
  days_allowed_after_event  = 14,                 # ...or up to 14 days after
  days_between_onset_death  = 30,                 # a death within 30 days of onset
  suffix                    = "_hosp",
  keep_pairs_pred           = TRUE
)

linked_hosp |>
  summarise(cases              = n(),
            linked_to_hospital = sum(!is.na(id_var_y_hosp)),
            admitted_in_window = sum(admission_outcome_hosp == "Admission")) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Cases linked to an acute hospital record, and admitted in the window")
```

```{r hospital-plot, fig.cap = "Case-to-hospital candidate-pair weights at threshold 8."}
murmuration_plot(linked_hosp, max_levels = 10)
```

***

## (*)> Step 9: Case-hospitalisation, ICU and case-fatality

The hospitalisation route adds `admission_outcome`, `first_admission_date`,
`icu_outcome` and `death_outcome` (here suffixed `_hosp`). Columns that come
only from the hospital extract (`diagnosis_codes_hosp` here) are blank for a
case whose matched admission falls outside the window, so they always describe
the in-window admission. The truth column repeats the same window rule using
`truth_id`, so the two can be compared.

```{r severity}
# the truth: an acute admission of the same person within the same window
truth_adm <- cases_blocked |>
  select(id_var, truth_id, onset_date) |>
  inner_join(hosp_clean |> select(truth_id, admission_date),
             by = "truth_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  filter(admission_date >= onset_date - 7,
         admission_date <= onset_date + 14)

linked_hosp <- linked_hosp |>
  mutate(admitted       = admission_outcome_hosp == "Admission",
         icu            = icu_outcome_hosp == "ICU Admission",
         died           = death_outcome_hosp == "Died",
         admitted_truth = id_var %in% truth_adm$id_var)

severity <- linked_hosp |>
  group_by(condition = diagnosis) |>
  summarise(cases          = n(),
            admitted       = sum(admitted),
            admitted_truth = sum(admitted_truth),
            icu            = sum(icu, na.rm = TRUE),
            died_30d       = sum(died, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(chr_pct       = round(100 * admitted / cases, 1),
         chr_truth_pct = round(100 * admitted_truth / cases, 1),
         cfr_pct       = round(100 * died_30d / cases, 2))

knitr::kable(severity, caption = "Case-hospitalisation (CHR) and case-fatality (CFR) by condition, linked vs truth")
```

```{r severity-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
chr_long <- bind_rows(
  severity |> transmute(condition, source = "Linked (threshold 8)", chr = chr_pct),
  severity |> transmute(condition, source = "Truth",                chr = chr_truth_pct)
)

ggplot(chr_long, aes(x = condition, y = chr, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Linked (threshold 8)" = aviary_cols[["satin"]],
                               "Truth" = aviary_cols[["wattle"]])) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Case-hospitalisation ratio (%)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r severity-details}
n_died_after_discharge <- linked_hosp |>
  filter(died, dod_hosp > first_discharge_date_hosp) |>
  nrow()

pct_covid_coded <- linked_hosp |>
  filter(admitted, diagnosis == "COVID-19") |>
  summarise(pct = round(100 * mean(grepl("U07[.]1|B97[.]2", diagnosis_codes_hosp)))) |>
  pull(pct)
```

Two details worth knowing:

- Deaths are recorded on the hospital episode, and `r n_died_after_discharge`
  of the linked 30-day deaths happened *after* discharge. `death_outcome`
  measures from onset, not from separation, so they are still counted.
- The window rule counts any acute admission that starts near onset. Of the
  linked COVID-19 admissions, `r pct_covid_coded`% carry a COVID-19 code
  (U07.1 or B97.2) anywhere on the episode. The published study required B97.2
  as an additional diagnosis [1]; filter on `diagnosis_codes` before linking if
  your definition needs it.

***

## (*)> Step 10: Vaccine effectiveness against hospitalisation

Both linkages hang off the same `id_var`, so they join directly. Among
COVID-19 cases, VE against hospitalisation is estimated as one minus the
risk ratio of admission, vaccinated versus not, from a log-link Poisson model
with robust (sandwich) standard errors -- the modified Poisson approach [5],
which estimates the same risk ratio as the log-binomial model of the published
study [1] but always converges.

```{r ve-data}
covid <- linked_hosp |>
  filter(diagnosis == "COVID-19") |>
  select(id_var, truth_id, age, onset_date, admitted, admitted_truth) |>
  inner_join(linked_cov |> select(id_var, vaccination_status_cov), by = "id_var") |>
  mutate(vaccinated   = vaccination_status_cov == "Vaccinated",
         hospitalised = as.integer(admitted),
         age_group    = cut(age, c(-Inf, 50, 65, 80, Inf), right = FALSE,
                            labels = c("<50", "50-64", "65-79", "80+")))

# The same exposure from the truth: a COVID-19 dose 14-182 days before onset
vaccinated_truth_ids <- covid |>
  select(id_var, truth_id, onset_date) |>
  inner_join(clutch_air |>
               filter(antigen == "COVID-19") |>
               select(truth_id, date_of_service),
             by = "truth_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  mutate(days_since_dose = as.numeric(onset_date - date_of_service)) |>
  filter(days_since_dose >= 14, days_since_dose <= 182) |>
  pull(id_var)

covid <- covid |>
  mutate(vaccinated_truth   = id_var %in% vaccinated_truth_ids,
         hospitalised_truth = as.integer(admitted_truth))

covid |>
  mutate(vaccination = if_else(vaccinated, "Vaccinated", "Unvaccinated"),
         admission   = if_else(hospitalised == 1, "admitted", "not admitted")) |>
  count(age_group, vaccination, admission, name = "cases") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "COVID-19 cases by age group, vaccination status and admission (linked data)")
```

Vaccinated cases are concentrated in the oldest age groups, where admission
is most common, so the crude comparison understates protection. Age
adjustment matters here:

```{r ve-models}
ve_fits <- list(
  "Crude (linked)"        = glm(hospitalised ~ vaccinated,
                                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = covid),
  "Age-adjusted (linked)" = glm(hospitalised ~ vaccinated + age_group,
                                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = covid),
  "Age-adjusted (truth)"  = glm(hospitalised_truth ~ vaccinated_truth + age_group,
                                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = covid)
)

ve_rows <- list()
for (model_name in names(ve_fits)) {
  fit   <- ve_fits[[model_name]]
  X     <- model.matrix(fit)
  bread <- summary(fit)$cov.unscaled
  meat  <- crossprod(X * (fit$y - fitted(fit)))
  se    <- sqrt(diag(bread %*% meat %*% bread))[2]   # robust SE, vaccination term
  b     <- coef(fit)[2]
  ve_rows[[model_name]] <- tibble(
    model = model_name,
    VE    = round(100 * (1 - exp(b)), 1),
    lower = round(100 * (1 - exp(b + 1.96 * se)), 1),
    upper = round(100 * (1 - exp(b - 1.96 * se)), 1)
  )
}
ve_table <- bind_rows(ve_rows)

knitr::kable(ve_table, caption = "VE (%) against hospitalisation among COVID-19 cases, 95% CI (robust)")
```

```{r ve-plot, fig.height = 2.8}
ve_table |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = rev(model))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = VE, y = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = aviary_cols[["slate"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.2, orientation = "y",
                colour = aviary_cols[["satin"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = aviary_cols[["chestnut"]]) +
  labs(x = "Vaccine effectiveness against hospitalisation (%)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The age-adjusted estimate from the linked data
(`r ve_table$VE[2]`%, 95% CI `r ve_table$lower[2]` to `r ve_table$upper[2]`)
sits close to the estimate from perfect linkage
(`r ve_table$VE[3]`%), so linkage error at this threshold barely moves the
answer. For comparison, the published regional Queensland study reported
69.9% (44.3--83.8) for a primary course and 81.8% (39.5--94.5) with a booster,
adjusting for age (<50/≥50), sex and Indigenous status [1]. The synthetic world
was generated with a weaker effect; the point here is the workflow, not the
number.

***

## (*)> Summary: the complete starling workflow

```{r workflow-summary, eval = FALSE}
library(starling)
library(mudnester)
library(dplyr)

# 0. Clean every source the same way -- and the AIR for ONE vaccine type only
cases <- clutch_cases |>
  mutate(onset_date = coalesce(onset_date, specimen_date)) |>
  clean_the_nest(data_type = "cases", id_var = "notification_id", ...)
air <- clutch_air |>
  filter(antigen == "COVID-19") |>
  clean_the_nest(data_type = "vaccination", lie_nest_flat = TRUE,
                 medicare = "medicare_card", medicare_irn = "medicare_irn", ...)
hosp <- clutch_hospital |>
  mutate(sex = case_when(sex == "Male" ~ "M", sex == "Female" ~ "F")) |>
  clean_the_nest(data_type = "hospital", ...)

# 1-3. Audit, Medicare validation (invalid -> NA), blocking
preflight(cases, air, linkage_vars = c("lettername1", "lettername2", "dob", "medicare10"))
cases <- cases |>
  check_medicare() |>
  mutate(medicare10 = if_else(medicare_valid %in% 0L, NA_character_, medicare10)) |>
  flock(block1_vars = c("gender", "birth_year"), birth_year_col = "dob")

# 4. Look before trusting a threshold (threshold_value defaults to 16)
first_pass <- murmuration(data_x = cases, data_y = air,
  linkage_type = "cohort2event", event_type = "vaccination",
  event_date = "onset_date", id_var = "id_var", blocking_var = "block1",
  compare_vars = c("lettername1", "lettername2", "dob", "medicare10"),
  keep_pairs_pred = TRUE)
perch(attr(first_pass, "pairs_pred"), n_records_primary = nrow(cases))
murmuration_plot(first_pass)

# 5-7. Link at the chosen threshold, one call per event stream, then validate
vax <- murmuration(data_x = cases, data_y = air, ..., threshold_value = 8,
  suffix = "_cov",
  vax_window = list(days_before = 14, days_after = 0, lookback_days = 182))
adm <- murmuration(data_x = cases, data_y = hosp, linkage_type = "cohort2event",
  event_type = "hospitalisation", ..., threshold_value = 8, suffix = "_hosp")

# 8-10. Join on id_var and analyse
cohort <- adm |>
  inner_join(vax |> select(id_var, vaccination_status_cov), by = "id_var")
```

## (*)> References

1. Smoll NR, Al Imam MH, Shulz C, Booy R, Khandaker G. The effectiveness of
   vaccination for preventing hospitalisation with COVID-19 in regional
   Queensland: a data linkage study. Med J Aust. 2023;219(4):162--165.
   doi:10.5694/mja2.52019. **Applied**: the notifications + hospital admissions
   + AIR design reproduced here, and the VE estimates used for comparison.
   **Precedent** for the probabilistic generalisation of its exact first name,
   last name and date-of-birth key.
2. Roughan WH, Cavanagh-Ochiai B, Barnekow D, Lottkowitz K, Schafer K, Camadoo
   L, Smoll NR. Infant respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunisation coverage
   in an Australian regional area, 1 May 2024 -- 31 October 2025. Commun Dis
   Intell. 2026;50. doi:10.33321/cdi.2026.50.031. **Precedent**: about 10% of
   its birth-register records needed weighted-score matching because of
   identifier and date-of-birth errors; inspecting the score distribution
   before fixing a threshold (Step 4) is the same discipline.
3. Fellegi IP, Sunter AB. A theory for record linkage. J Am Stat Assoc.
   1969;64(328):1183--1210.
4. van der Laan DJ. reclin2: a toolkit for record linkage and deduplication.
   R J. 2022;14(2):320--328.
5. Zou G. A modified Poisson regression approach to prospective studies with
   binary data. Am J Epidemiol. 2004;159(7):702--706.
